# An exact positive-semidefinite criterion for prescribed planar sector areas

This note eliminates all auxiliary vertices from the finite convexity
system in `candidate 697de064a9368ba1`.
It is an ordinary planar statement. It does not preserve compatibility
between different mixed-integer fibers.

## 1. Data and matrix

Let m>=3 and let nonzero points P_1,...,P_m lie on distinct rays in cyclic
order about zero, with every consecutive angular gap strictly below pi.
All indices below are cyclic. Set

    D_i=det(P_i,P_(i+1))>0,
    E_i=det(P_(i-1),P_(i+1)),
    kappa_i=D_(i-1)+D_i-E_i.

Prescribe finite sector areas A_i>=D_i/2. Define

    t_i=2 A_i/D_i>=1,       a_i=t_i-1,
    h_i=a_i/(D_i t_i)=1/D_i-1/(2 A_i)>=0,
    b_i=kappa_i/(D_(i-1)D_i).

Let L be the symmetric m by m matrix determined by its quadratic form

    x^T L x=sum_i b_i x_i^2-sum_i h_i(x_i+x_(i+1))^2.       (1)

Thus L_ii=b_i-h_(i-1)-h_i and its cyclic adjacent off-diagonal entries
are -h_i. Equation (1), rather than an ambiguous entry convention, is
the definition even for small m.

**Theorem.** There exists a planar convex body K containing zero in its
interior, with boundary ray points exactly P_i and sector areas exactly
A_i, if and only if L is positive semidefinite.

When the condition holds, K can be chosen to be a polygon with at most
2m vertices, at most one extra vertex between consecutive prescribed
ray points. In particular three lines and their six endpoints require
at most twelve vertices.

## 2. The finite geometric system being eliminated

The audited fixed-sector replacement and its convexity calculation give
the following exact condition. There must exist u_i,v_i>0 with

    u_i+v_i=t_i,
    D_i a_(i-1)/u_(i-1)+D_(i-1) a_i/v_i<=kappa_i.          (2)

The additional point in sector i is V_i=u_i P_i+v_i P_(i+1).
For zero excess a_i=0 one may take u_i=v_i=1/2.

For clarity, the local convexity expression in (2) is obtained directly
by dividing

    det(P_i-V_(i-1),V_i-P_i)>=0

by u_(i-1)v_i>0. The result is exactly (2). At each extra point V_i,
convexity follows from t_i>=1. The sector gauges glue convexly across
P_i precisely under (2); the source note proves this without assuming
a realizing body. Conversely an arbitrary realizing body has the exact
one-extra-vertex replacement with the same data, so (2) is necessary.

The remainder of this note proves the algebraic equivalence of (2)
and positive semidefiniteness of (1), including all zero-excess cases.

## 3. Harmonic edge charges

For a_i>0 define

    r_i=a_i/(D_i u_i),       s_i=a_i/(D_i v_i).

Then (2) is equivalent to node budgets and an edge identity:

    r_(i-1)+s_i<=b_i,
    r_i s_i/(r_i+s_i)=h_i.                              (3)

At a_i=0 put r_i=s_i=0. Instead of the identity in (3), allow the closed
convex edge condition

    r_i>=h_i, s_i>=h_i,
    (r_i-h_i)(s_i-h_i)>=h_i^2.                          (4)

For h_i>0 this is exactly r_i s_i/(r_i+s_i)>=h_i, with both variables
strictly greater than h_i. It is a convex set: it is the epigraph
r_i>=h_i+h_i^2/(s_i-h_i), s_i>h_i, and the displayed inequalities show
that it is closed in the plane. For h_i=0 it is simply the nonnegative
quadrant.

The relaxation from equality to (4) loses nothing. If h_i>0 and its
harmonic value is H_i>=h_i, multiply both r_i,s_i by h_i/H_i<=1.
This lowers both adjacent budget charges and makes the harmonic value
exactly h_i. Then set

    u_i=a_i/(D_i r_i),       v_i=a_i/(D_i s_i).

Their sum equals (a_i/D_i)/h_i=t_i. They are strictly positive. For
h_i=0 reduce the two charges to zero and choose u_i=v_i=1/2. This
constructs (2) exactly from any feasible relaxed charges.

## 4. Closed budget set and a self-contained separation argument

Let B be the set of vectors beta in R^m for which there are edge
charges satisfying (4) and r_(i-1)+s_i<=beta_i. The set B is nonempty,
convex and closed, and is upward closed in each coordinate.

Nonemptiness follows by taking r_i=s_i=2h_i. Convexity follows from
convexity of each edge set and the linear node inequalities. To prove
closedness, suppose beta^(j) in B converges to a finite beta. All chosen
charges are nonnegative, with r_i^(j)<=beta_(i+1)^(j) and
s_i^(j)<=beta_i^(j). They are uniformly bounded, so a subsequence of
all finitely many charges converges. Their limits satisfy the closed
edge conditions and node inequalities. Thus beta belongs to B.

For this nonempty closed convex upward set,

    b in B  iff  theta.b>=inf_(beta in B) theta.beta
                    for every theta>=0.                   (5)

Only the reverse implication requires proof. If b is outside B, choose
a nearest point b* in B. Existence follows by restricting minimization
to a closed bounded ball that contains one candidate with finite
distance. Convexity and the squared-distance derivative along segments
give

    (b*-b).(beta-b*)>=0 for every beta in B.

Set theta=b*-b. Since b*+t e_i belongs to B for all t>=0, every
theta_i is nonnegative. Moreover

    inf_(beta in B) theta.beta>=theta.b*
       =theta.b+|theta|^2>theta.b.

This contradicts the inequalities in (5), proving the equivalence.
No strict feasibility or dual attainment assumption is needed.

## 5. Exact dual edge cost

The infimum in (5) separates over the edges. On edge i its cost is

    theta_(i+1) r_i+theta_i s_i.

For h_i>0 write r_i=h_i+x and s_i=h_i+y, where x,y>0 and xy>=h_i^2.
The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives the exact infimum

    inf [theta_(i+1) r_i+theta_i s_i]
       =h_i(sqrt(theta_i)+sqrt(theta_(i+1)))^2.             (6)

When both coefficients are positive, take
x=h_i sqrt(theta_i/theta_(i+1)) and
 y=h_i sqrt(theta_(i+1)/theta_i) to attain equality. If one coefficient
vanishes, the same value is approached by letting the uncharged
variable grow and the charged one tend down to h_i. When both vanish
the cost is zero. For h_i=0 both charges can be zero and (6) remains
valid. The infimum, rather than an asserted minimizer in a zero-weight
case, is all that (5) uses.

Therefore (2) is feasible exactly when

    sum_i b_i theta_i
       >=sum_i h_i(sqrt(theta_i)+sqrt(theta_(i+1)))^2
                   for every theta_i>=0.                   (7)

The simultaneous finite reconstruction follows from the closed budget
set in Section4, even though some individual zero-weight dual infima
are not attained.

## 6. Copositivity is positive semidefiniteness here

Set x_i=sqrt(theta_i). Condition (7) says x^T L x>=0 for every x>=0.
All off-diagonal entries of L are nonpositive. Consequently for every
real vector x,

    x^T L x >= |x|^T L |x|,

because the diagonal terms agree and each off-diagonal product has
coefficient at most zero. Nonnegativity on the nonnegative orthant
therefore gives nonnegativity on all real vectors. Conversely positive
semidefiniteness certainly implies (7). This proves the theorem.

The test consists of one explicit finite matrix and no unresolved
optimization over inserted vertices. Its scope is still the exact
ordinary ray/sector data. It does not establish the conjectured global
mixed-integer depth bound or a shape classification.

## 7. A direct finite reconstruction from a smallest eigenvector

There is a shorter constructive proof of the matrix equivalence, which
also records explicit auxiliary vertices. Join adjacent indices by an
edge exactly when h_i>0. The matrix L is block diagonal on the connected
components of this graph.

Suppose L is positive semidefinite. In each block choose a unit vector
minimizing its Rayleigh quotient. A minimizer exists on the compact unit
sphere and satisfies the eigenvector equation for the least eigenvalue,
by differentiating under the norm constraint. Replacing its entries by
their absolute values cannot increase the quadratic form, because every
off-diagonal entry is nonpositive. Thus a nonnegative minimizing
eigenvector exists. In a connected block it is strictly positive: if
one entry were zero, the corresponding eigen-equation would force all
positive-edge neighbors to vanish, and connectivity would force the
entire vector to vanish. For a singleton block choose the entry one.

The least eigenvalues are nonnegative. Concatenate these positive block
vectors into w>0. Then Lw>=0 coordinatewise. On each positive edge put

    r_i=h_i(1+w_i/w_(i+1)),
    s_i=h_i(1+w_(i+1)/w_i).

Their harmonic value is exactly h_i, and the inequality (Lw)_i>=0 says
exactly r_(i-1)+s_i<=b_i. Set both charges to zero on a zero edge. The
corresponding explicit sector coordinates are

    u_i=t_i w_(i+1)/(w_i+w_(i+1)),
    v_i=t_i w_i/(w_i+w_(i+1))                 when h_i>0,
    u_i=v_i=1/2                              when h_i=0.

They are finite and strictly positive, and they satisfy (2). Hence they
construct the claimed polygon directly, even when L is singular or has
several components.

Conversely, feasible harmonic charges and node slacks

    delta_i=b_i-r_(i-1)-s_i>=0

give the exact Gram identity

    x^T L x=sum_i delta_i x_i^2
       +sum_(i:h_i>0) (s_i x_i-r_i x_(i+1))^2/(r_i+s_i).

This proves positive semidefiniteness directly for every real x. Zero
edges contribute nothing. Thus neither separation nor any positive
spectral gap is necessary for the equivalence. Sections4-6 additionally
provide its useful dual scalar inequality for every nonnegative weight
vector.
